title: Rain boots
stem:
Rain boots are made of rubber.

Which two properties of rubber make it suitable?
key: Some jobs need two properties. Rain boots must be waterproof and flexible.

options.text: It is waterproof and it lets light through.
options.pick: Rubber is waterproof, and any second property seems to do.
options.why: Boots don't need to let light through. They need to bend when you walk.

options.text: It absorbs water and it is flexible.
options.pick: Rubber boots get wet, so rubber seems to soak up water.
options.why: Rubber is waterproof: it does not absorb water. That keeps your feet dry.

options.text: It is waterproof and it is flexible.
options.pick: List what boots must do: keep water out, and bend as you walk.
options.why: Rubber is waterproof, so water stays out, and flexible, so the boots bend without breaking.

options.text: It is waterproof. The boots do not need to bend.
options.pick: Keeping the rain out is the main job.
options.why: Your feet bend at every step, so the boots must be flexible too.

title: What floats?
stem:
Ali put four objects into water. The table shows what happened.

Which statement is correct?
figure:
ObjectIn water
large wooden logfloats
small steel nailsinks
corkfloats
small glass marblesinks
key: Whether an object floats depends on what it is made of, not on how big or heavy it is.

options.text: Whether an object floats depends on what it is made of.
options.pick: Compare the big log with the tiny nail.
options.why: The large log floats and the small nail sinks. It is the material that matters.

options.text: Big objects sink and small objects float.
options.pick: Big things look heavy.
options.why: The large log floats, and the small nail and marble sink.

options.pick: Heavy seems to mean it will go down.
options.why: The wooden log is the heaviest object here, and it floats.

options.text: The nail sinks because metal is strong.
options.pick: Metal is strong, and strong things seem to sink.
options.why: Strength is about holding loads without breaking. It doesn't decide whether something floats.

title: A bathroom window
stem:
A bathroom window must let light in, but people outside must not be able to see in clearly.

Which material is most suitable?
key: Frosted glass lets some light through: the room is bright, but people cannot see in clearly.

options.pick: Windows are usually made of clear glass.
options.why: Clear glass lets most light through, so people could see in clearly.

options.pick: The window needs some light, but not a clear view.
options.why: Frosted glass lets some light through. The room is bright, but people can't see in clearly.

options.pick: Wood would stop people seeing in.
options.why: Wood lets no light through, so the bathroom would be dark.

options.pick: Metal is strong and blocks the view.
options.why: Metal lets no light through, so the bathroom would be dark.

title: The torch test
stem:
Siti shone a torch through sheets of four materials, W, X, Y and Z, onto a screen. The table shows how bright the screen was behind each sheet.

Which two materials could be wood and metal?
figure:
MaterialScreen behind the sheet
Wbright
Xdark
Ydim
Zdark
key: Wood and metal let no light through, so the screen behind them is dark.

options.pick: They are the first and third in the table.
options.why: Light reached the screen behind W and Y. Wood and metal let no light through.

options.pick: Picked one bright and one dark.
options.why: W let most light through. Wood and metal both let none through.

options.pick: Which materials let no light reach the screen?
options.why: Wood and metal let no light through, so the screen behind them is dark.

options.pick: Dim seems close enough to dark.
options.why: A dim screen means some light got through Y. Wood and metal let none through.

title: A strong shelf
stem:
Three strips, P, Q and R, were tested. The results are shown.

Which strip is most suitable for a shelf that holds heavy books?
figure:
StripWeights held before breakingBent without breaking?
P1yes
Q8no
R3yes
key: A shelf needs strength: the ability to hold a heavy load without breaking.

options.text: P, because it bends without breaking
options.pick: Bending without breaking sounds like a good thing.
options.why: A shelf doesn't need to bend. It needs to hold a heavy load: P is the weakest.

options.pick: What must a shelf do? Which strip held the most weights?
options.why: Q held the most weights without breaking, so it is the strongest.

options.text: R, because it is strong and flexible
options.pick: Having two good properties seems better than one.
options.why: The shelf needs strength only. R held fewer weights than Q.

options.text: None of them, because a strong material must also bend
options.pick: Strong and flexible seem to go together.
options.why: They are different properties. Q is strong but not flexible, and that is fine for a shelf.

title: Bending three strips
stem:
Mei bent a rubber strip, a fabric strip and a ceramic tile. Only one broke.

Which one broke, and why?
key: Ceramic is not flexible: it breaks when bent. Rubber and fabric are flexible.

options.text: The rubber strip, because rubber is waterproof
options.pick: Rubber feels firm.
options.why: Rubber is flexible: it bends without breaking.

options.text: The fabric strip, because fabric is absorbent
options.pick: Fabric is soft and seems weak.
options.why: Fabric is flexible: it bends without breaking.

options.text: The ceramic tile, because ceramic is not strong
options.pick: It broke, so it seems weak.
options.why: Breaking when bent is about flexibility, not strength. Ceramic is not flexible.

options.text: The ceramic tile, because ceramic is not flexible
options.pick: Which material breaks when it is bent?
options.why: Ceramic is not flexible, so it breaks when bent.

title: The water-drop test
stem:
A drop of water was put on each of four materials, A, B, C and D. The table shows what happened.

Which two materials could be used for the cover of an umbrella?
figure:
MaterialWhat the drop of water did
Asoaked in
Bstayed on top
Csoaked in
Dstayed on top
key: A waterproof material does not absorb water: the drop stays on top.

options.pick: An umbrella cover must not let water soak in.
options.why: The drops stayed on top of B and D, so they are waterproof.

options.pick: The water disappeared into them, so they seem to stop it.
options.why: The water soaked into A and C. They are absorbent, so the umbrella would let water through.

options.pick: Picked the first two in the table.
options.why: A is absorbent. Only B and D are waterproof.

options.text: All four, because water touched all of them
options.pick: All the materials got water on them.
options.why: The test shows which ones keep water out. Only B and D did.

title: A towel
stem: Why is a towel made of fabric?
key: Fabric is absorbent: it soaks up water.

options.pick: Towels are used with water.
options.why: A waterproof towel couldn't dry you. Fabric is absorbent.

options.pick: Towels are pulled and rubbed.
options.why: Drying you is the main job, and that needs a material that soaks up water.

options.text: Fabric is absorbent: it soaks up water.
options.pick: What does a towel have to do?
options.why: A towel dries you by soaking up water, so it must be absorbent.

options.pick: Some fabrics are thin.
options.why: Letting light through has nothing to do with drying you.

title: Which object?
stem: Which object is made of a material that is waterproof and lets most light through?
key: Clear glass is waterproof and lets most light through.

options.pick: Flower pots hold water.
options.why: Ceramic lets no light through.

options.pick: Thin cotton lets a little light through.
options.why: Cotton fabric is absorbent, not waterproof.

options.pick: Rulers are smooth.
options.why: Wood lets no light through.

options.pick: Which material is both waterproof and lets most light through?
options.why: Clear glass is waterproof and lets most light through.

title: A fair torch test
stem:
Siti wants to compare how much light passes through four materials, using a torch and a screen.

What must she keep the same?
key: In a fair test, change only the material. Keep everything else the same.

options.text: The distances from the torch to the sheet and from the sheet to the screen, and the thickness of each sheet
options.pick: What could change the result apart from the material?
options.why: Keep everything the same except the material, so any difference comes from the material.

options.text: The type of material in each sheet
options.pick: Everything in a fair test seems to stay the same.
options.why: The material is what she is testing, so it must change.

options.pick: It is part of the set-up.
options.why: That is the result she observes, not something she keeps the same.

options.text: Nothing. She can use a different torch for each sheet.
options.pick: Any torch gives light.
options.why: A brighter torch would make a sheet look clearer. She must use the same torch.

title: Some light
stem: Which material lets some light through, but not most?
key: Frosted glass lets some light through.

options.pick: Glass lets light through.
options.why: Clear glass lets most light through.

options.pick: Thin wood seems to let a little light in.
options.why: Wood lets no light through.

options.pick: Which one makes things look blurry behind it?
options.why: Frosted glass lets some light through.

options.pick: It is very thin.
options.why: Clear food wrap lets most light through.

title: A dark box
stem:
A box must keep out all light.

Which material is most suitable?
key: Wood, metal and rubber let no light through.

options.pick: Plastic boxes are common.
options.why: Clear plastic lets most light through.

options.pick: It blocks the view.
options.why: Frosted glass still lets some light through.

options.pick: Which material lets no light through?
options.why: Wood lets no light through, so the box stays dark.

options.pick: Paper seems to block light.
options.why: Tracing paper lets some light through.

title: A block and a paper clip
stem:
A big wooden block and a small metal paper clip were put into water. The block floated and the paper clip sank.

What does this show?
key: Whether an object floats depends on what it is made of, not on its size.

options.text: Whether an object floats depends on what it is made of, not on its size.
options.pick: The bigger object floated. What does that tell you?
options.why: The big wooden block floated and the tiny metal clip sank, so size didn't decide it.

options.text: Big objects float and small objects sink.
options.pick: That is what happened here.
options.why: A small cork floats, and a big rock sinks. The material decides.

options.pick: The paper clip was small and sank.
options.why: A small cork floats. Size doesn't decide.

options.text: The paper clip sank because it was heavier than the block.
options.pick: Things that sink seem heavy.
options.why: The block is much heavier than the clip, and it floated.

title: A fishing float
stem:
A float for a fishing line must stay on the surface of the water.

Which material is most suitable?
key: Cork floats. Glass, clay and metal sink, however small the piece.

options.pick: It is tiny, so it seems it would float.
options.why: Glass sinks, however small it is.

options.pick: Which material floats?
options.why: Cork floats, so it stays on the surface.

options.pick: Clay can be shaped easily.
options.why: Clay sinks.

options.pick: It is big enough to see on the water.
options.why: Metal sinks.

title: Which one sinks?
stem: Which of these sinks in water?
key: Cork, Styrofoam and most wood float. Metal, glass, clay and rock sink.

options.pick: It is big.
options.why: Styrofoam floats, even in a big box.

options.pick: It is long and heavy.
options.why: Most wood floats.

options.pick: Corks go in bottles of liquid.
options.why: Cork floats.

options.pick: Which material sinks?
options.why: Glass sinks, even a small marble.

title: Flexible and waterproof
stem: Which material is both flexible and waterproof?
key: Rubber is flexible and waterproof.

options.pick: Which material bends without breaking and keeps water out?
options.why: Rubber is flexible and waterproof.

options.pick: Ceramic cups hold water.
options.why: Ceramic is not flexible. It breaks when bent.

options.pick: Fabric is flexible.
options.why: Cotton fabric is absorbent, not waterproof.

options.pick: Glass keeps water in a jar.
options.why: Glass is waterproof but not flexible.

title: About glass
stem: Which statement about clear glass is correct?
key: Clear glass lets most light through and is waterproof. It is not flexible, and it sinks.

options.pick: Thin glass seems bendy.
options.why: Glass is not flexible. It breaks when bent.

options.text: It lets most light through and is waterproof.
options.pick: Think of a window on a rainy day.
options.why: Clear glass lets most light through and does not absorb water.

options.pick: Glass gets wet in the rain.
options.why: Water stays on the surface of glass. Glass is waterproof.

options.pick: Glass bottles bob on water.
options.why: Glass sinks. A bottle floats only because of the air inside.

title: A bench seat
stem: Why is the seat of a bench often made of wood?
key: Wood is strong, so it can hold people up without breaking.

options.pick: Any property of wood seems to do.
options.why: Wood lets no light through, and a seat doesn't need to.

options.pick: A seat should feel comfortable.
options.why: The seat must hold people up without breaking. That needs strength.

options.pick: Benches are outdoors in the rain.
options.why: Absorbing water doesn't help a seat. Holding a load does.

options.pick: What must a seat do?
options.why: Wood is strong, so it can hold people's weight without breaking.

title: A cracked flower pot
stem:
A clay flower pot cracks when someone tries to bend it.

Which property of ceramic explains this?
key: Ceramic is not flexible: it breaks when bent.

options.pick: Bending without breaking is which property?
options.why: Ceramic is not flexible, so it breaks when bent.

options.pick: It broke, so it seems weak.
options.why: Breaking when bent is about flexibility. Strength is about holding loads.

options.pick: Flower pots get watered.
options.why: Absorbing water doesn't explain why it cracked when bent.

options.pick: That is true of ceramic.
options.why: It is true, but it has nothing to do with bending.

title: Two drops of water
stem:
A drop of water is put on a cotton T-shirt and another on a plastic bag.

What happens?
key: Cotton is absorbent; plastic is waterproof.

options.text: It stays on top of the cotton and soaks into the plastic.
options.pick: Mixed up which one is waterproof.
options.why: Cotton is absorbent and plastic is waterproof, so it is the other way round.

options.pick: Water soaks into most things.
options.why: Plastic is waterproof, so the drop stays on top.

options.text: It soaks into the cotton and stays on top of the plastic.
options.pick: Which material is absorbent, and which is waterproof?
options.why: Cotton is absorbent, so it soaks the water up. Plastic is waterproof, so the drop stays on top.

options.text: It stays on top of both.
options.pick: Both are smooth enough.
options.why: Cotton is absorbent, so the drop soaks in.

title: A fair floating test
stem:
Ravi wants to find out which of four materials float.

What must he keep the same?
key: In a fair test, change only the material. Keep everything else the same.

options.pick: Everything in a fair test seems to stay the same.
options.why: The material is what he is testing, so it must change.

options.text: The size and shape of each block, and the water he uses
options.pick: What could change the result apart from the material?
options.why: Keep everything the same except the material, so the result depends only on the material.

options.pick: It is part of the test.
options.why: That is the result he observes, not something he keeps the same.

options.text: The colour of each block, and nothing else
options.pick: Colour is easy to see.
options.why: Colour doesn't matter. Size, shape and the water do.

title: What strength means
stem: Which statement about strength is correct?
key: Strength is the ability to take a load without breaking. Flexibility is the ability to bend without breaking.

options.text: A strong material can bend without breaking.
options.pick: Strong things seem tough in every way.
options.why: That describes flexibility.

options.text: A strong material must also be waterproof.
options.pick: Good properties seem to come together.
options.why: Strength and waterproofness are different properties. Wood is strong but not waterproof.

options.text: A material that bends easily must be strong.
options.pick: Bending without breaking sounds strong.
options.why: Bending without breaking is flexibility. A flexible material can be weak.

options.text: A strong material can hold a heavy load without breaking.
options.pick: Recall what "strength" means.
options.why: Strength is the ability to take a load without breaking.
